http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/survi.text: A man who survived a ferry disaster that claimed at least 46 lives on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba told the AFP news agency on Thursday how he watched helplessly as people tried to save themselves, with his best friend and seven of his relatives among the dead.The overloaded government ferry, a vital link for villagers and fish traders around the vast lake, overturned in choppy waters on Tuesday in one of the country's worst passenger boat disasters."Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top," Chance Siyamavhu said at a memorial service in the lakeside town of Kariba close to the border with Zambia.Perched on the upended boat, he watched as passengers struggled to survive, unable to save them."When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the life jackets but most of them did not even know how to use them," the 45-year-old told AFP. "Most people could not make it.""Our relatives were swept in another direction and they sank because we were not in a position to help them," he said.Dozens of mourners gathered in front of 44 coffins at the emotional service, as police announced that the death toll had risen to 46."The names of the victims who perished in the accident will be released in due course," a police statement said.Officials say the boat was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.The civil protection unit said 77 people were rescued and there were fears that other passengers may be unaccounted for.Survivors said they had pleaded for the captain to turn back as the boat took on water.Anymore Chambati, who had been a security official on the vessel, told AFP he had tried to hand out life jackets as the boat began to sink."I managed to only give not more than 10," he said. "The ferry engines were filled with water because of the heavy winds and eventually they failed, save for one."

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-far-righ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NqWo AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund (r) congratulated Tobias Rausch (l) on his election as parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement First thing in the morning, about 500 people gathered on Cathedral Square in the center of Magdeburg, the capital of the state of Saxony-Anhalt , to send a clear message that October 6 is not just another ordinary day. "Against Forgetting — Fascism Must Remain a Crime," read one of their banners. "No cooperation with the far right," read another. Directly across from the imposing cathedral, in the state parliament building on the other side of the square, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) was elected as speaker of the state parliament at 12:40 p.m. He received 48 votes — 9 more than the number of seats the AfD holds in the state parliament. And this marks a turning point not only for Saxony-Anhalt but for all of Germany. For the first time since the end of World War II , a German state parliament has elected as its president a representative of a party that the Office for the Protection of the Constitution , the domestic intelligence agency, has classified as right-wing extremist. 'The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is a right-wing extremist party' The parliament's inaugural session was opened by Eva von Angern, a member of the socialist Left Party and the senior-most member of the parliament, who had earlier been outside participating in the demonstration across the square. She noted that only a few women in German history had held such a high office. Among them, Von Angern said, was communist Clara Zetkin, who served as senior member of the Reichstag in 1932 — shortly before the Nazis seized power. Nobody in the AfD caucus showed any support for these words. "Human dignity shall be inviolable," Von Angern then quoted from Germany's Basic Law . This includes, she added, people of different genders, worldviews, religions and skin colors. And she quoted former Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker. "He said: 'One expresses one's own dignity by respecting the dignity of others.'" Once again, no one in the AfD expressed any enthusiasm. Allegations of nepotism against Rausch Tobias Rausch, a 35-year-old real estate agent, is little known outside of Saxony-Anhalt. Many observers describe him as relatively approachable, and he describes himself as "not a hardliner." However, his name made headlines nationally at the beginning of the year when numerous AfD politicians were accused of nepotism . Rausch himself admitted to employing several of his friends from his soccer club in his legislative office. That did not prevent his caucus from nominating him as president of the state legislature. Officially, the office is the highest-ranking position in the state. After his election as parliamentary speaker, Rausch asserted: "I will not serve in this office as the speaker of a single parliamentary group, but as the speaker of all parliamentary groups." He added: "Rules must apply even when the majority changes." After AfD's record result: voices from Saxony-Anhalt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A large AfD bloc — in the center of the chamber Not everyone in the state parliament trusts this gesture of goodwill. During the first session following the election, a glance at the seating arrangement of the packed plenary chamber underscores the sheer force with which the AfD intends to shape policy here going forward: The AfD parliamentary caucus — composed of 37 men and two women — had taken its seats in the center, keeping a firm gaze on the lectern. The fact that this can be intimidating is clearly intentional. Not everyone in the state parliament trusts this gesture of goodwill. During the first session following the election, a glance at the packed plenary chamber underscores the sheer force with which the AfD intends to shape policy here going forward: The parliamentary caucus — composed largely of men — seated itself prominently in the center where they could keep a firm eye on the lectern. Observers remarked that this can be intimidating. Unlike in other parliaments, where the far-right party would normally sit far to the right, it has positioned the "old parties" that it despises — namely the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the socialist Left Party and the environmentalist Greens — around the edges. The AfD was able to push this seating arrangement through in preliminary talks before the state parliament convened to vote. The message is clear: We are the center. A new era has begun in Saxony-Anhalt. A regional election that drew international attention The election that took place on September 6 of this year in Saxony-Anhalt was certainly the most closely watched regional election in Germany in many years. Several hundred journalists, including several from international media, traveled to Magdeburg for the election. Among the 1.7 million eligible voters in this German state, located between the Elbe River and the Harz Mountains, one thing was clear months before election day: the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which has been partially classified as right-wing extremist — would emerge as the strongest party. Some polls even predicted that the party would secure an absolute majority of the votes. In the end, the AfD garnered 39 of the 83 seats, just shy of the 42 seats it would have needed for an absolute majority. Added together, the CDU, the Left Party, the SPD and the Greens also come to a combined total of 39 seats. The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht , holds just five seats and yet could be the deciding factor in whether AfD's top candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, can actually become the state premier. The BSW had announced that it would vote for Rausch as parliamentary speaker, but not for Siegmund as head of the state government. Nevertheless, Siegmund plans to stand for election in the state parliament in December. It will again take place by secret ballot. Siegmund has been displaying confidence, saying he intends to win in the first round of voting. And if he fails, he intends to call fresh elections. Why Germany's political center is losing ground To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video On this point, the new parliamentary speaker, Tobias Rausch, commented on private TV channel RTL the morning before his election: "If we don't have a majority in the first round of voting, we won't have a majority for the rest of the legislative term either — in that case, it means the parliament doesn't want us to govern." Whatever happens, Saxony-Anhalt is facing turbulent times ahead. This article was originally written in German. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge.text: Image caption, Bechi was recorded at an event earlier this year by undercover BBC reporters By Endang Nurdin and Rebecca Henschke ,Â BBC Eye Â and Â BBC News Indonesia Published 8 October 2026 A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early. Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher. A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know. On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief. "I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC. The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations. But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review. That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison. Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions". "We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said. Image caption, Ira Puspitasari (right), one of several women who accused Bechi of rape and abuse, said she was "amazed" to hear the news For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication. "I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said. Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15. "I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said. She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her. She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened". Catching My Teacherâ¯ Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Watch on iPlayer Listen on Sounds Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube , external . Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful. "It's like nothing ever happened," she said. Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation. Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings". He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases. Figure caption, Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java. He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest. Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student. The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response. https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Lena Schilling is one of 50 MEPs, 46 of them women, who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes. Photograph: APA-Images/Alamy View image in fullscreen Lena Schilling is one of 50 MEPs, 46 of them women, who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes. Photograph: APA-Images/Alamy Online abuse ‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action Lena Schilling of Austrian Greens says images are ‘digital violence against women’ and a threat to democracy Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent Sun 18 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 00.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Austrian MEP has spoken out about her experience of being “stripped naked” online without her consent and has urged the EU to take action, as a report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content. Lena Schilling of the Green party said she had learned last month about nude deepfakes of herself circulating online. When she opened the links, she found herself staring at images from one of her first ever press conferences – but the images had been digitally altered to remove her clothing. It was a shocking twist on a defining moment of her career. “I felt disgusted,” she said. “I remember how nervous I was and how much I had prepared for the press conference. And then to see someone using this image in a way aimed at harming and humiliating me was really hard to grasp.” Schilling is one of 50 MEPs – 46 of them women – who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes, according to a report by Agora Digitale Transformation (ADT). View image in fullscreen Schilling said some of the other female MEPs who were also targeted had expressed fears about speaking out. Photograph: Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty The Berlin-based thinktank, which alerted Schilling to the presence of the images online, said the finding laid bare how deepfake pornography had become a “systemic threat to women in European politics”. An earlier ADT report found that 138 female parliamentarians from 22 EU countries had been affected, and that women were 33 times more likely than their male colleagues to be depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography. Schilling described the images as a form of “digital violence against women” piled on top of the already disproportionate amount of sexist abuse, harassment and violence that women in politics faced. The result was a potent threat to democracy, she said: “These things make going into politics even harder than it is already. Just imagine what would happen to our society if more and more women disappear from public life.” Schilling said she had spoken to some of the other female MEPs targeted, but they had expressed fears about coming forward. “But there’s nothing to be ashamed of. People misused your photos, you did nothing wrong,” she said. “And I think that’s the moment when you say: ‘OK, this has to stop.’” The sentiment was captured in a recent letter to the EU initiated by Schilling and the German Green MEP Terry Reintke. Signed by 119 MEPs, it called on officials to ensure that a forthcoming ban on apps and websites that use AI to undress women, scheduled to take effect across the EU on 2 December, would be paired with mechanisms capable of enforcing the prohibition. “A ban on paper protects no one until it is enforced,” the letter said, pointing to the widespread use of “nudifier” apps in which photos of women can be undressed with just one click. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Elon Musk’s xAI sues Minnesota over law banning ‘nudification’ technology Read more “Its purpose is humiliation and control over women’s bodies, and its effect is to make public life more hostile for female politicians,” the letter said. “Every young woman considering a political career now must factor in that this could happen to her.” Schilling said the aim was to push national authorities to close any loopholes or workarounds that would allow the apps to continue to function in the EU. “We were stripped naked without our consent,” she said. “This cannot become the new normal.” The call for action was why she had decided to speak up, she said, in the hope that sharing her story would convince member states to crack down on tech companies for which this sort of digital violence could be a viable business model. “It’s quite simple,” she said. “Every woman who wants to run for office should be able to do so without being afraid of being undressed against her will.” Explore more on these topics Online abuse Deepfake European Union Europe Violence against women and girls Sexual harassment Gender news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
